topics.title: The UK, Great Britain and the British Isles
topics.where: A civil servant on her lunch break outside the Palace of Westminster, London.
lines: Great Britain is an island, shared by England, Scotland and Wales.
The United Kingdom is a country: Great Britain plus Northern Ireland. In full, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
The British Isles is a geographers' name for the whole group, Ireland included. Many people in Ireland dislike it, so you'll often hear 'Britain and Ireland' or 'these islands' instead.
Ireland is a separate, independent country. The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands belong to the Crown but aren't part of the UK either.
'British' covers everyone in the UK, and plenty also, or instead, call themselves English, Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish or Irish.

topics.title: Westminster and the Crown
topics.where: The same civil servant, outside the Palace of Westminster, London.
lines: The UK is a constitutional monarchy. King Charles III is head of state; elected politicians do the governing.
The UK Parliament sits at Westminster: the elected House of Commons, with 650 MPs, and the House of Lords, which isn't elected.
The Prime Minister is whoever can command a majority in the Commons, usually the leader of the biggest party.
There's no single written constitution. It's a mix of laws, court rulings and conventions, which is either wonderfully flexible or alarmingly vague, depending who you ask.
Ireland, next door, has a written constitution from 1937 that can only be changed by a referendum, and an elected President.

topics.title: Devolution
topics.where: A guide at the Pierhead in Cardiff Bay, or a researcher at Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh.
lines: In 1997 Scotland and Wales voted in referendums for their own elected bodies. Scotland said yes by 74%. Wales said yes by 50.3%, a very close shave.
The Scottish Parliament and the National Assembly for Wales were first elected in May 1999. The Welsh one has been called the Senedd since 2020.
They make laws on things like health, schools and transport. Westminster keeps defence, foreign affairs and most of the big money levers.
Northern Ireland's Assembly came out of the 1998 Agreement, and shares power between its communities.
England has no parliament of its own: Westminster makes England's laws. London has had an elected mayor since 2000, and other city regions have since followed.

topics.title: Power-sharing at Stormont
topics.where: A student at Belfast City Hall.
lines: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Parliament Buildings, Stormont, on the east side of Belfast. It has 90 members.
The First Minister and deputy First Minister share one joint office with equal power. So far one has always come from a unionist party and one from a nationalist party.
Some big votes need support from both unionist and nationalist members, so neither side can simply outvote the other.
When the parties can't agree, the Assembly stops working. It has been suspended or stalled several times since 1998.

topics.title: Ireland: from the Free State to the Republic
topics.where: A history lecturer at the Custom House, Dublin.
lines: From 1801 all of Ireland was part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
After the 1916 Rising and the War of Independence of 1919 to 1921, the Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed in December 1921.
The Irish Free State came into being on 6 December 1922. Six counties in the north-east stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland, set up in 1921.
The Treaty split Irish nationalism, and a civil war followed in 1922 and 1923.
A new constitution in 1937 named the state Éire, or Ireland, in English. It became a republic in 1949, and left the Commonwealth.
Today Ireland and the UK are close neighbours and big trading partners. They even joined the European Economic Community on the same day, 1 January 1973.

topics.title: The Troubles and the Good Friday Agreement
topics.where: A retired shipwright and a teacher at Belfast City Hall.
lines: From the late 1960s to 1998, Northern Ireland lived through the Troubles. More than 3,500 people were killed, over half of them civilians.
At its heart was a dispute over which country Northern Ireland should belong to, tangled up with civil rights, discrimination, policing and fear on all sides.

Unionists, mostly from a Protestant background, want Northern Ireland to stay in the UK. Nationalists, mostly from a Catholic background, hope for a united Ireland. Plenty of people are neither, or a bit of both.
The Agreement was reached on Good Friday, 10 April 1998. In May, 71% voted yes in Northern Ireland and 94% in the Republic.
At its core is consent: Northern Ireland stays in the UK unless a majority there votes otherwise. People born there can be British, Irish or both, and hold either passport or both.
Unionists tend to call it the Belfast Agreement, nationalists the Good Friday Agreement. Same document, same peace.

topics.title: Derry, Londonderry and other names
topics.where: A local historian in the Guildhall, Derry~Londonderry.
lines: Derry comes from the Irish Doire, an oak grove. A royal charter of 1613 made it Londonderry, after the City of London companies who paid for the walls and the plantation.
Nationalists mostly say Derry; many unionists say Londonderry. The council is Derry City and Strabane, and you'll see both names on signs.
Some write Derry~Londonderry or Derry/Londonderry, which is why a local radio presenter nicknamed it Stroke City.

Northern Ireland is 'the North' or 'the Six Counties' to some, 'Ulster' or 'the Province' to others. The old province of Ulster has nine counties, and three of them, Donegal included, are in the Republic.
Which is how Donegal, the most northerly county in Ireland, ends up in the South.

topics.title: The open border
topics.where: A walker from Derry on the border road into Donegal, on the Glenveagh route.
lines: The border between Northern Ireland and the Republic runs for about 500 kilometres, through fields, rivers, loughs and, here and there, somebody's farm.
During the Troubles it had army checkpoints, and many small roads were closed. Since the Agreement you can cross without noticing, apart from the speed signs going metric.
Thousands cross it every day for work, school, shopping and family.
After Brexit it became the only land border between the UK and the European Union, and keeping it open was the hardest knot of the lot.

topics.title: The Common Travel Area
topics.where: Bernie's sister Áine in Donegal Town, or the plaque at Holyhead's ferry terminal.
lines: Since 1923 the UK and Ireland, along with the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, have formed the Common Travel Area.
British and Irish citizens can live, work, study and get healthcare in each other's countries, and there's no passport check on the Irish land border.
Irish citizens in the UK can vote in UK elections, and British citizens living in Ireland can vote for the Dáil, Ireland's parliament.
It's older than the EU and it outlived Brexit. Ferries and airlines still want photo ID, and anyone who isn't British or Irish needs the right papers.

topics.title: Brexit
topics.where: A haulier in the ferry terminal at Cairnryan.
lines: On 23 June 2016 the UK voted to leave the European Union, by 52% to 48%.
England and Wales voted to leave. Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain, Scotland by 62% and Northern Ireland by 56%.
Gibraltar, which had been in the EU along with the UK, voted 96% to remain.
The UK left on 31 January 2020, and the transition period ended on 31 December 2020.
People argued about trade, sovereignty, migration and money then, and still do. Ireland stayed in the EU, so the Irish border became a border between the UK and the EU.

topics.title: The Protocol and the Windsor Framework
topics.where: The haulier at Cairnryan, or the plaque in the ferry terminal there.
lines: Nobody wanted checkpoints back on the Irish border. So the Northern Ireland Protocol, part of the deal the UK left under, kept Northern Ireland following EU rules for goods.
That moved the checks to the Irish Sea: goods coming from Great Britain are checked at ports such as Belfast and Larne.
Many unionists felt it put a border inside their own country. Many nationalists, and plenty of businesses, saw it as the price of keeping the land border open.
In February 2023 the UK and the EU agreed the Windsor Framework: a green lane with lighter checks for goods staying in Northern Ireland, and a red lane for goods going on into the EU.
It also added a 'Stormont brake', which lets the Assembly object to new EU rules for goods.

topics.title: The Crown Dependencies
topics.where: An advocate at the Royal Court in St Helier, Jersey.
lines: The Isle of Man, the Bailiwick of Jersey and the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which takes in Alderney, Sark and Herm, are Crown Dependencies.
They aren't part of the UK and were never in the EU. They make their own laws and set their own taxes, and the UK looks after their defence and foreign relations.
Jersey has its States Assembly, Guernsey its States of Deliberation, and Man has Tynwald, which says it is the oldest continuous parliament in the world.
They send no MPs to Westminster. The King is their head of state: Lord of Mann on the Isle of Man, and toasted as Duke of Normandy in the Channel Islands.
The Isle of Man let some women vote in 1881, decades before women got the vote in Britain.

topics.title: The Overseas Territories
topics.where: A volunteer at the Gibraltar Museum.
lines: There are 14 British Overseas Territories, from Gibraltar and Bermuda to the Falklands, St Helena and a slice of Antarctica.
They aren't part of the UK. Most of the inhabited ones elect their own government, a Governor represents the King, and the UK handles defence and foreign policy.
Since 2002 most of their people have been full British citizens.
Spain still claims Gibraltar, and Argentina the Falklands. Both places have voted by huge margins to stay British.
Most use a currency tied to the pound or the US dollar. The two bases on Cyprus use the euro.

topics.title: The Commonwealth
topics.where: A Commonwealth Games volunteer near Westminster, London.
lines: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of 56 countries, most once ruled by Britain, with about a third of the world's people.
Members are equal and free to leave. Ireland left in 1949, and Mozambique and Rwanda joined without ever having been British colonies.
King Charles III is its Head, but most members are republics or have monarchs of their own. Fourteen countries besides the UK still have him as their King.
Its secretariat is at Marlborough House in London, and most people know it for the Commonwealth Games, every four years.

topics.title: The Chagos Islands
topics.where: A Chagossian woman on a heritage visit, at Naval Party 1002 on Diego Garcia.
lines: The Chagos Archipelago, in the Indian Ocean, was governed from Mauritius until 1965, when Britain split it off as the British Indian Ocean Territory.
Mauritius became independent in 1968. Between 1967 and 1973 the Chagossians were removed from their islands to make way for a US military base on Diego Garcia.
Mauritius claims the islands. In 2019 the International Court of Justice gave an advisory opinion that Britain should end its administration there; the UK said the opinion was not binding.
In October 2024 the UK and Mauritius announced a deal in principle for Mauritius to take sovereignty, with the base on Diego Garcia staying.
Chagossians, many now living in Mauritius, Seychelles and Crawley in West Sussex, don't all want the same thing, and many say they were never properly asked.
